claims.text: Cryogenic dynamic tensile loading promotes further evolution and growth of interstitial-driven local chemical order domains in an FCC high-entropy alloy.
Enlarged LCO domains promote dislocation cross-slip and change deformation from planar slip to wavy slip.
The LCO-mediated change in slip behavior simultaneously raises yield strength and work hardening while preserving ductility.
A modified CoCrFeMnNi alloy containing interstitial solutes can serve as the proposed incipient-LCO material.
The controlled comparison is cryogenic tensile deformation, for example at 77 K, versus room-temperature tensile deformation of the same alloy.
High-resolution microscopy combined with quantitative phase or chemical mapping can be used to track LCO-domain evolution during deformation.
The structural mediator consists of dynamically enlarged, interstitial-driven LCO domains forming dense laths in the FCC matrix.
Cryogenic specimens will have higher yield strength than room-temperature specimens.
Cryogenic specimens will exhibit more pronounced work hardening than room-temperature specimens.
Cryogenic specimens will retain ductility relative to the room-temperature baseline.
Cryogenic specimens will show enhanced and coarsened LCO domains.
The enhanced LCO domains will correlate with increased dislocation cross-slip activity.
At room temperature, LCO evolution is minimal.
Room-temperature deformation is dominated by conventional planar slip without the enhanced cross-slip seen during cryogenic deformation.
The mechanism should apply across ambient-to-cryogenic temperatures to FCC high-entropy alloys engineered with interstitial solutes for incipient LCO formation.
Deformation twinning may concurrently contribute to cryogenic work hardening.
Failure to observe increased LCO growth or cross-slip under cryogenic loading would falsify the proposed LCO-mediated mechanism.
Failure to observe enhanced yield strength and work hardening relative to room temperature would falsify the predicted mechanical outcome.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes dynamic loading, but no dynamic or high-strain-rate value is defined; the comparison changes temperature while only stating that strain rate is controlled. Thus a specifically dynamic-loading effect cannot be isolated from a temperature effect.

The falsification rule treats absent LCO/cross-slip and absent mechanical enhancement as equivalent, although the hypothesis acknowledges that twinning or other mechanisms could enhance the mechanical response even when the proposed LCO pathway is absent.
